name: MuckRock
purpose: Platform for filing, tracking and publishing US public-records requests, handling agency correspondence, fee and appeal workflows, and a public archive of completed requests and released documents.
journalism_use_case: Managing a public-records practice rather than individual requests: file across many agencies, track deadlines and appeals, and search the archive of what other requesters have already obtained — which frequently answers your question without a new request.
pros: Deadline and appeal tracking is the capability that turns sporadic requests into a sustained practice, which is where public-records reporting actually produces results
The public archive of completed requests is a research asset in itself: searching it shows what an agency has released before and how it responds, which shapes how you frame a request
Open source under a journalism non-profit whose mission is records access, so incentives align and the service is unlikely to pivot away
Operated as a working service alongside DocumentCloud, so requests and released documents land in a usable publishing pipeline
cons: US only, and the workflow encodes US FOIA and state public-records conventions

The platform publishes requests and responses by default, which is right for accountability and wrong for a sensitive investigation where the request itself tips off the target — embargo options exist but the default matters
Self-hosting is a substantial Django deployment and almost never the right choice given the service exists
Service fee structure for filing (postage, fees) and account tiers were not verified in this survey
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: the repository is live and non-archived under MuckRock's maintenance alongside DocumentCloud. MuckRock's operation of a public records service with a substantial public archive is well documented.
assessment: Use the service for US records work, with an explicit decision per request about publication timing — and file sensitive requests directly with the agency instead, because a public request is a notification to your target. For your profile the underused half is the archive: searching prior requests to the same agency is faster than filing, and it reveals the agency's refusal patterns before you commit to a request that will be denied.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived under MuckRock's institutional maintenance, supporting an operating public service alongside DocumentCloud. The service is the primary artefact.
licence: AGPL-3.0 (project licensing — confirm from the repository licence file)
model_or_data_licence: Released documents are public records; MuckRock's service terms govern platform use and were not verified here.
licence_restrictions: Copyleft would apply to a modified hosted instance; immaterial for using the service.
costs: Service fees and account tiers NOT verified in this survey — MuckRock has historically charged for filing credits with free tiers for some users. Confirm before planning a filing programme. Self-hosting would be a major Django deployment. Estimate.
privacy: Requests and responses are published by default, which discloses what you are asking and of whom. Embargo options exist but the default is publication — a deliberate accountability choice that conflicts with investigative secrecy.
alternatives: Filing directly with agencies for sensitive requests
Alaveteli or Froide for non-US jurisdictions with similar publish-by-default models
FOIA Machine-style self-managed tracking in a spreadsheet for a small programme
blockers: Publish-by-default discloses requests; US jurisdiction only; service fees unverified

name: bellingcat/EDGAR
purpose: Tool for searching the US Securities and Exchange Commission's EDGAR full-text and filing-index systems, retrieving filings by company, form type, date and text content.
journalism_use_case: Searching the full text of US corporate filings for a name, address or phrase: finding every SEC filing that mentions a particular individual, shell company or address is a standard step in corporate investigation and is awkward through EDGAR's own interface.
pros: Full-text search across filings is the capability that matters: a name appearing in an obscure exhibit is often the link an investigation needs, and EDGAR's web interface makes that hard to find systematically
Built by Bellingcat for investigators, so the interface assumes a research task rather than a financial-analysis one
GPL-3.0 with a tagged release (v2.1.2, 2025-05-15) and a clear scope
Free access to a rich official dataset — SEC filings are public and unusually detailed about corporate structure and related parties
cons: Maintenance has slowed: last push and release both 2025-05-15, eighteen months before this survey, and EDGAR's interfaces do change
US-registered entities only, so it covers a specific slice of global corporate activity — though an important one, since many international structures touch US markets
Full-text coverage in EDGAR does not extend uniformly across all historical filings, so an absence is not evidence
Narrow tool: it finds filings, and reading and interpreting them is the work
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 216 stars, release v2.1.2 (2025-05-15) with the last push the same day, GPL-3.0. Session 1's candidate path bellingcat/edgar-tool is a 404; the correct repository is bellingcat/EDGAR (verified 2026-11-17).
assessment: Useful for the specific task of full-text searching SEC filings, with the caveat that eighteen months without maintenance against a changing official interface warrants a liveness check before you rely on it. For your profile the alternatives are worth knowing: edgartools is more actively maintained and offers richer parsing, so I would test both and prefer whichever currently works, treating this as the simpler option for pure search.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2025-05-15, latest release v2.1.2 published the same day, 216 stars, GPL-3.0. Eighteen months without activity on a tool that depends on an official interface which does change — declining rather than dormant, but verify it still works.
model_or_data_licence: SEC filings are US government-published public records.
licence_restrictions: Copyleft on the tool; immaterial for internal use.
costs: No fee. EDGAR access is free with fair-use rate limits. Negligible compute.
privacy: Queries go to the SEC, disclosing your search terms to a US government system. Unremarkable for most work; consider it if the subject is sensitive.
alternatives: edgartools for a more actively maintained Python interface with richer parsing
sec-edgar-downloader for bulk filing retrieval
EDGAR's own full-text search for one-off queries
blockers: Eighteen months without maintenance against a changing official interface

name: edgartools
purpose: Python library for accessing SEC EDGAR data with a high-level API over companies, filings and financial statements, parsing structured data out of filings including XBRL financial facts.
journalism_use_case: Going beyond finding filings to extracting their content: pull the actual financial figures, related-party disclosures, officer lists and ownership tables from filings into structured data, which is what turns a corporate investigation from reading PDFs into analysis.
pros: Structured extraction of financial facts and filing sections is the substantive advantage: analysing a company's disclosures across years requires parsed data, not documents
High-level API means common tasks (get a company's filings, extract a statement) are a line or two rather than a parsing project
Actively maintained with a frequent release cadence, which matters because EDGAR's structures and XBRL conventions change
Open source and free against a free official data source, so the whole corporate-filings capability costs nothing but time
cons: Parsing financial filings is intrinsically error-prone: XBRL tagging quality varies by filer, and a mis-extracted figure that looks plausible is the characteristic failure — any published number needs checking against the filing
US-registered entities only
Single-maintainer project, so continuity depends on one person despite the good current cadence
The high-level API hides parsing decisions, which is convenient and means you may not notice when an extraction is wrong
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented from the metadata sweep: the repository is live and non-archived with an active release cadence. No journalism deployment verified.
assessment: Adopt it for structured corporate-filings work — it is the better-maintained of the two EDGAR options here and the structured extraction is where the analytical value is. For your profile the discipline that matters is verification: extract at scale to find the pattern, then open the underlying filing and confirm every figure that reaches print, because XBRL tagging errors by filers are common and the library cannot detect them.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived with an active release cadence from a single committed maintainer. Maintenance is current; the bus factor is the residual risk.
licence: MIT (project licensing — confirm from the repository licence file)
model_or_data_licence: SEC filings are US government-published public records.
costs: No fee. EDGAR access free with fair-use rate limits. Negligible compute.
privacy: Requests go to the SEC, disclosing the companies you are researching to a US government system.
alternatives: bellingcat/EDGAR for simpler full-text search, with its maintenance caveat
sec-edgar-downloader for bulk document retrieval without parsing
Arelle for rigorous XBRL processing where financial precision is critical

name: Arelle
purpose: Open-source XBRL platform for loading, validating and querying XBRL financial reports against taxonomies, with validation plugins for regulatory filing rules in several jurisdictions.
journalism_use_case: Rigorous processing of structured financial filings: load a company's XBRL report, validate it against the regulator's taxonomy, and extract facts with their full context (period, unit, dimension) — which is how you avoid the misreading that makes a financial story wrong.
pros: Validation against official taxonomies is the distinguishing capability: it tells you whether a filing is internally consistent and correctly tagged, which is both a data-quality check and occasionally a story
Handles the full XBRL context model (periods, units, dimensions), so extracted facts carry the qualifications that make them meaningful — the detail that simpler extractors drop
Covers multiple jurisdictions' filing rules through plugins, so it extends beyond US EDGAR to European and other regulatory regimes
Long-established open-source project with institutional involvement from the XBRL community
cons: XBRL is a genuinely complex standard and Arelle exposes that complexity rather than hiding it — the learning curve is the main cost and it is substantial for a journalist
Designed for filing-preparation and regulatory validation, so the workflow assumes accounting expertise rather than investigative questions
Heavy and slow relative to simpler extractors; for 'what was revenue in 2024' edgartools is far quicker
Maintenance cadence is steady rather than brisk, consistent with a mature standards-oriented project
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented from the metadata sweep: the repository is live and non-archived with continuing development. Arelle's standing in the XBRL community is well established; journalism use is specialist and unverified here.
assessment: Reach for it only when financial precision is central and the jurisdiction's XBRL taxonomy matters — a story turning on how a company classified a liability, for example. For your profile the realistic division is edgartools for extraction and exploratory analysis, Arelle when a figure must be defensible to an accountant, and an actual accountant consulted before publication either way. The validation capability is the reason it is in the catalogue.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived with continuing but modest development, consistent with a mature standards-implementation project. Classified stable-low: the standard evolves slowly and so does the implementation.
licence: Apache-2.0 (project licensing — confirm from the repository licence file)
model_or_data_licence: Taxonomies are published by regulators under their own terms.
costs: No fee. Compute for loading and validating large filings; taxonomies are free downloads. The real cost is the expertise to use it correctly. Estimate.
privacy: Local processing. Taxonomy downloads contact regulators' servers.
alternatives: edgartools for faster, more accessible US filing extraction
Direct XBRL parsing for a single known filing structure
An accountant, which for a financial story is not an alternative but a requirement

name: sugartrail
purpose: Tool that builds a network graph from UK Companies House data, following officers, addresses and company relationships outward from a starting entity to map connected corporate structures.
journalism_use_case: Mapping a UK corporate network from one starting point: begin with a company or director and follow officers, shared addresses and appointments to reveal the cluster of entities around them — the standard method for exposing shell-company networks and the addresses that host hundreds of them.
pros: Automates the manual click-through that UK corporate investigation otherwise requires, which is the difference between mapping ten companies and mapping four hundred
Address-based traversal is particularly productive: a single accommodation address hosting hundreds of companies is a recurring and reportable pattern that this surfaces directly
Built by Bellingcat for investigators, so the traversal logic reflects how corporate-network investigation actually proceeds
Companies House data is openly licensed and free via API, so the whole capability costs nothing
cons: UK only, and tightly coupled to Companies House's data model, so it is a template rather than a tool elsewhere
Network expansion grows combinatorially: an unconstrained traversal from a busy address produces an unusable graph, so hop limits and filtering are essential and require judgement

Shared officers and addresses indicate association, not wrongdoing — a company-formation agent's address legitimately hosts thousands of companies, and publishing a network as evidence of impropriety would be wrong
Small project; verify liveness and API compatibility before relying on it
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented from the metadata sweep: the repository is live and non-archived under Bellingcat's maintenance. Bellingcat's published UK corporate-network investigations are the relevant context for the method's productivity.
assessment: Adopt it for UK corporate work and treat the output as a map requiring interpretation. For your profile the two disciplines are hop limits (constrain the traversal or drown) and the formation-agent caveat (a shared address is usually a service provider, not a conspiracy). The transferable value is the method: any jurisdiction with an open company register supports the same traversal, and building it for your region is a contained project with high investigative return.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived under Bellingcat's maintenance, with modest activity typical of a focused investigative tool. Classified stable-low; verify Companies House API compatibility before relying on it.
licence: MIT (project licensing — confirm from the repository licence file)
model_or_data_licence: UK Companies House data is published under the Open Government Licence, which permits reuse with attribution.
licence_restrictions: Code permissive as published. Companies House data requires OGL attribution — straightforward but a real publication obligation.
costs: No fee. Companies House API is free with rate limits. Negligible compute. Estimate.
privacy: Queries go to Companies House, disclosing the companies you are investigating to a UK government system. Public-register research, so unremarkable.
alternatives: Companies House API directly with your own traversal logic
OpenCorporates for multi-jurisdiction corporate data, with its own access terms
Building an equivalent traversal for another jurisdiction's open register — the transferable approach
blockers: UK only; shared addresses and officers indicate association, not wrongdoing

name: ethereum-etl
purpose: Tool that exports Ethereum blockchain data — blocks, transactions, token transfers, logs, contracts — into CSV, JSON or a data warehouse for SQL analysis.
journalism_use_case: Following cryptocurrency flows with your own data rather than a commercial analytics platform: export the transactions and token transfers around a set of addresses into a database and analyse the flows yourself, which is both cheaper and more defensible than citing a vendor's attribution.
pros: Gives you the raw data, so your analysis is reproducible and your conclusions are yours — unlike commercial blockchain-analytics tools whose attribution methods are proprietary and unexaminable
Export to a warehouse means SQL analysis over blockchain data, which is far more tractable for a data journalist than an API-by-API approach
Open source and free against public blockchain data, so the only cost is infrastructure
Established tooling in the blockchain data ecosystem with a clear scope
cons: Requires an archive node or a node-provider endpoint: running your own archive node is a serious storage commitment, and using a provider means disclosing your queries to them
Addresses are pseudonymous, and attributing an address to a person or organisation is the hard part that this does not help with — exactly where commercial tools add their (proprietary) value
Data volume is very large: exporting a meaningful slice of Ethereum history is terabyte-scale, so scoping matters
Ethereum-specific, with sibling projects for other chains of varying maintenance quality
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented from the metadata sweep: the repository is live and non-archived. The blockchain-etl family is established in the data-engineering side of blockchain analysis; journalism use is plausible but unverified here.
assessment: Use it when a story turns on cryptocurrency flows and you want analysis you can defend — the reproducibility argument against commercial attribution tools is strong, since you cannot explain in print what a vendor's proprietary clustering did. For your profile the honest limitation is attribution: the blockchain tells you what moved where, and connecting an address to a named person requires conventional reporting (exchange records, leaks, admissions). Scope your export tightly and budget node access.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived with modest ongoing activity. Classified stable-low: the export logic is largely stable because the data model is, so low velocity is less concerning than it would be for a scraper.
licence: MIT (project licensing — confirm from the repository licence file)
model_or_data_licence: Blockchain data is public by design.
costs: No software fee. The real costs are node access — running an archive node is multi-terabyte storage, and a commercial node provider charges per request (not priced here) — plus warehouse storage for exports. This is the most infrastructure-heavy item in this segment. Estimate.
privacy: If you run your own node, your queries disclose nothing. Using a commercial node provider discloses which addresses you are investigating to that provider — a meaningful exposure when the subject may be a well-resourced actor.
alternatives: BlockSci for academic-grade blockchain analysis with its own infrastructure requirements
GraphSense for a platform-oriented approach to cryptocurrency flow analysis
Commercial analytics (Chainalysis class) for attribution, accepting proprietary methods and cost
blockers: Requires archive-node access or a commercial provider; address attribution is not solved by this tool

name: GraphSense
purpose: Open-source cryptocurrency analytics platform providing address clustering, entity tagging, transaction-flow analysis and an API across several blockchains.
journalism_use_case: The open alternative to commercial blockchain analytics: cluster addresses into entities, apply tags, and trace flows between them — giving you the entity-level view that raw transaction data lacks, with clustering heuristics you can inspect rather than trust.
pros: Address clustering is the capability that makes blockchain analysis useful, and having it open means the heuristics are inspectable — which is the difference between a defensible published claim and citing a black box
Multi-blockchain coverage with an API, so it is a platform rather than a single-chain script
Academic origin (AIT) with published methodology, so the clustering approach can be cited and critiqued
Open source, so a newsroom is not dependent on a commercial analytics subscription whose methods it cannot examine
cons: Heavy infrastructure: ingesting and clustering blockchain data requires substantial compute and storage, realistically a cluster rather than a VM — this is the main barrier and it is high
Clustering heuristics are probabilistic: co-spending and other patterns suggest common control without proving it, and publishing a cluster as 'this entity' overstates the evidence
Entity tagging depends on tag data whose sources and quality vary, and a wrong tag propagates into a wrong attribution
Commercial entity (Iknaio) involvement, so the open-core boundary and direction warrant checking before you build on it
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented from the metadata sweep: the repository is live and non-archived. GraphSense's academic lineage and published methodology are documented by the project; I verified no newsroom deployment.
assessment: Worth knowing about rather than deploying, unless cryptocurrency is a sustained beat and you have real infrastructure — the ingestion cost is the obstacle. For your profile the realistic path on a crypto story is ethereum-etl for targeted flow analysis plus conventional reporting for attribution, with GraphSense considered only if clustering at scale becomes central. If you do publish cluster-based claims, state the heuristic and its limits explicitly, because the clustering is the contestable step.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived, but the project spans several repositories with a commercial entity involved and no clear single release cadence. Open-core boundary and continuity could not be assessed from metadata — classified Uncertain rather than inferred.
licence: MIT (project licensing — confirm from the repository licence file; open-core model with commercial involvement)
model_or_data_licence: Tag datasets have their own provenance and terms, which matter because tags drive attribution.
licence_restrictions: Permissive as published; verify which components are open and which are commercial before designing around it.
costs: No software fee. Infrastructure is substantial: blockchain ingestion and clustering at scale needs a cluster with large storage — the dominant cost and the practical barrier for a newsroom. Estimate.
privacy: Self-hosted analysis keeps your investigation private, which is the main advantage over commercial platforms that see every address you query.
alternatives: ethereum-etl plus your own analysis for targeted flow work at far lower cost
Commercial analytics for attribution, accepting proprietary methods, cost and query disclosure
Collaboration with an academic group that already operates a GraphSense instance
blockers: Substantial ingestion infrastructure required; clustering heuristics are probabilistic and must be stated as such
